lv-dc-drop.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Chapter 9 Table 8 (used as a copper-resistance reference, not as a low-voltage code).

assumptions.name: Application tolerance
assumptions.value: LED 3% / marine 10% / RV 5% / audio 2%

fall-protection-clearance.formula: Required clearance = free-fall + decel + worker_height + harness_stretch + safety_factor. Compared against the user-entered actual clearance below the anchor. Negative remaining clearance flags FAIL.
fall-protection-clearance.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.502 (Fall protection systems criteria) by section. ANSI Z359 (Fall Protection and Fall Restraint) by name. Manufacturer connector-decel benchmarks from data/crosswalks/fall-protection-benchmarks.json.
fall-protection-clearance.freeAccess: 29 CFR 1926.502 free at ecfr.gov. ANSI Z359 licensed; manufacturer guides free at each manufacturer site.
fall-protection-clearance.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
fall-protection-clearance.editionNote: 29 CFR 1926.502 plus the ANSI/ASSP Z359 maxima: Z359.13-2013 lanyard deployment (48 in for a 6 ft free fall, 60 in for 12 ft) and Z359.14-2021 self-retracting arrest distance (42 in for Class 1 and Class 2; the 2012 edition allowed 24 in Class A / 54 in Class B). Manufacturer clearance charts govern the device in use.

assumptions.name: Default free-fall
assumptions.value: 6 ft for personal fall arrest (PFAS)

assumptions.name: Default decel
assumptions.value: 4.0 ft for a 6 ft free-fall shock-absorbing lanyard (48 in maximum deployment; OSHA's 3.5 ft is the system limit, not the labeled stroke) / 3.5 ft for an overhead SRL (the 42 in arrest-distance cap)
assumptions.source: ANSI/ASSP Z359.13-2013; ANSI/ASSP Z359.14-2021 for the SRL

assumptions.name: Default worker height
assumptions.value: 5 ft from D-ring to feet

assumptions.name: Default safety factor
assumptions.value: 1 ft margin

hearing-protector-nrr.formula: C-weighted measurement: attenuation = NRR. A-weighted measurement under OSHA methods: attenuation = NRR - 7. OSHA field guidance halves that adjusted value. NIOSH derating applies to the labelled NRR by protector type - x0.75 earmuffs, x0.50 slow-recovery formable earplugs, x0.30 all other earplugs - and an A-weighted measurement then takes 7 dB off the derated value. Exposure at the ear = TWA - effective attenuation.
hearing-protector-nrr.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95 Appendix B (Methods for Estimating the Adequacy of Hearing Protector Attenuation), a US federal regulation in the public domain; derating factors from NIOSH, Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Noise Exposure (1998).
hearing-protector-nrr.freeAccess: 29 CFR is published in full at no cost by OSHA and the eCFR; the NIOSH criteria document is published at no cost by CDC/NIOSH.
hearing-protector-nrr.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hearing-protector-nrr.editionNote: The number on the package is never the protection, and Appendix B says why in one step people skip. The NRR comes off a C-WEIGHTED measurement directly, but where the measurement is A-weighted - which is what a dosimeter reports and what everyone actually has - Appendix B directs that you 'subtract 7 dB from the NRR' first, for spectral uncertainty, and then subtract the remainder. That single step is worth 7 dB every time, and measuring in dBC rather than dBA is therefore worth 7 dB of paper protection on the same job. On top of that sits derating, which is NOT Appendix B text and is labelled as such here. The 50% field adjustment is OSHA enforcement guidance rather than regulation. The type-specific factors are NIOSH's: earmuffs subtract 25% from the labelled NRR, slow-recovery formable earplugs subtract 50%, and all other earplugs subtract 70%. NIOSH then computes the effective level by subtracting the derated NRR from a C-weighted exposure, or the derated NRR minus 7 dB from an A-weighted one, so both families take the 7 dB on a dosimeter reading (until 2026-10-03 this tile left it off the NIOSH methods). The practical consequence is large: an NRR 29 pre-molded earplug on a 98 dBA job credits about 1.7 dB under NIOSH and leaves 96.3 dB at the ear, where the package number would have suggested 69. The dual-protection bonus is an editable input defaulted to the 5 dB commonly applied under OSHA Technical Manual guidance; NIOSH recommends double protection above a 100 dBA TWA without quantifying the gain, and two protectors never add their ratings because the second is working against sound arriving by bone conduction and around the first. Not checked: whether the exposure is measured correctly, which is the TWA calculation and a separate tile; the noise spectrum, since the NRR is a single number standing in for a curve and low-frequency noise defeats it; fit, which is what derating exists to approximate and what fit-testing measures directly; wearing time, where removing a protector for a few minutes of an eight-hour shift costs more than any derating; protector condition, size, and insertion; and the audiometric testing, training, and recordkeeping the standard also requires, including the provision that an employee who has experienced a significant threshold shift must have attenuation sufficient to reduce exposure to a TWA of 85 dB. An attenuation estimate, not a hearing conservation program.

assumptions.name: C-weighted measurement
assumptions.value: the NRR is subtracted directly

assumptions.name: A-weighted measurement
assumptions.value: subtract 7 dB from the NRR, then subtract the remainder from the TWA

assumptions.name: OSHA 50% derating
assumptions.value: halves the adjusted value; enforcement guidance, not Appendix B text

assumptions.name: NIOSH derating
assumptions.value: earmuffs -25%, slow-recovery formable earplugs -50%, all other earplugs -70% of the labelled NRR
assumptions.source: NIOSH Criteria for a Recommended Standard, Occupational Noise Exposure (1998)

assumptions.name: NIOSH and the 7 dB
assumptions.value: an A-weighted exposure takes the derated NRR minus 7 dB
assumptions.source: NIOSH Criteria for a Recommended Standard, Occupational Noise Exposure (1998)

assumptions.name: Dual protection
assumptions.value: editable bonus, defaulted to 5 dB per OSHA Technical Manual guidance; not from Appendix B

conduit-thermal-expansion.formula: delta_L = coefficient x (run_length_ft x 12) x temperature_change; an expansion fitting is required once delta_L reaches the 1/4-inch (0.25 in) trigger, sized for that travel. PVC coefficient 3.38e-5 in/in/deg-F.
conduit-thermal-expansion.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). 352.44 (expansion fittings for rigid PVC conduit).
conduit-thermal-expansion.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.

assumptions.name: PVC coefficient
assumptions.value: the bundled 3.38e-5 in/in/deg-F coefficient is the public PVC physical property underlying NEC Table 352.44; the manufacturer's published coefficient governs

manning-pipe-capacity.formula: English Manning V = (1.486 / n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2); full-bore circular pipe R = D/4, A = (pi/4) D^2, Q = V A; Q_gpm = 448.831 Q_cfs.
manning-pipe-capacity.edition: Manning equation; n-values from USGS WSP-2339 (public domain).
manning-pipe-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
manning-pipe-capacity.editionNote: The discharge side of the Manning equation for a circular pipe flowing full: V = (1.486/n) R^(2/3) sqrt(S) with the full-bore hydraulic radius R = D/4 and area A = (pi/4) D^2, so Q = V A. This is the inverse of the manning-slope tile, which solves the same equation for the slope; here the diameter, slope, and roughness are given and the capacity and velocity returned. The roughness n is from the standard tables (PVC 0.009, cast iron / concrete 0.013, corrugated metal 0.024). Because Q scales with sqrt(S), doubling the slope raises the capacity only about 1.41x. It assumes a steady, uniform (normal-depth) full flow; it does not compute the partial-flow depth, and a circular pipe carries a few percent more than full-bore at about 0.94 depth (pipe-partial-flow-depth gives the partial-flow depth). A design aid, not a substitute for a licensed engineer's design; the engineer of record and the local plumbing/sewer code govern.

assumptions.name: Full-bore hydraulic radius
assumptions.value: R = D/4, A = (pi/4) D^2 for a circular pipe flowing full

assumptions.name: Roughness
assumptions.value: n from the standard tables (PVC 0.009, concrete 0.013, corrugated metal 0.024), entered by material

assumptions.name: Uniform full flow
assumptions.value: steady normal-depth full flow; the partial-flow depth is separate

approach-delta-t.formula: Approach = condenser saturation temperature − outdoor temperature (cooling). Delta-T = T_return_air − T_supply_air. Targets compared against manufacturer commissioning guide ranges.
approach-delta-t.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.

assumptions.name: Typical delta-T
assumptions.value: 16–22 °F across the indoor coil for cooling

braking-distance.formula: Braking distance d = v² / (2 × g × (μ + grade)) + reaction_distance. Reaction distance = v × t_reaction. g = 32.2 ft/s².
braking-distance.edition: Classical kinematics; AASHTO 'Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets' (Green Book) by name.
braking-distance.freeAccess: AASHTO Green Book licensed; kinematics free in physics texts.
braking-distance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
braking-distance.editionNote: Physics, with AASHTO Green Book design values named for comparison: 2.5 s perception-reaction time and 11.2 ft/s² deceleration. The tile's 1.5 s and friction defaults are alert-driver and reconstruction values, not the Green Book's design values.

assumptions.name: Typical friction μ (enter one)
assumptions.value: 0.7 dry asphalt / 0.4 wet / 0.2 ice; the AASHTO Green Book's stopping sight distance uses a fixed 11.2 ft/s² deceleration (about μ = 0.35) instead
assumptions.source: common accident-reconstruction values; AASHTO Green Book for the design deceleration

assumptions.name: Default reaction time
assumptions.value: 1.5 s unless user supplies, an alert driver expecting to stop; the AASHTO Green Book design perception-reaction time is 2.5 s, which adds 1.0 s x 1.467 ft/s per mph (about 81 ft at 55 mph)
assumptions.source: AASHTO Green Book (2.5 s design value)

floor-level-change.formula: change in level <= 1/4 in may be vertical; > 1/4 in and <= 1/2 in must be beveled at a slope no steeper than 1:2, so the required run = 2 x the rise; > 1/2 in must be ramped under 405 or 406, so the run = rise x the ramp run per rise (12 for 1:12). Carpet pile <= 1/2 in. Openings must not pass a sphere over 1/2 in, and elongated openings run perpendicular to the dominant direction of travel.
floor-level-change.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 302.2, 302.3, 303.2, 303.3, and 303.4. A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
floor-level-change.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
floor-level-change.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
floor-level-change.editionNote: Three thresholds govern a change in level, and the last one is a cliff rather than a step. Up to 1/4 in the change may be VERTICAL - a square edge with no transition at all, which the standard permits rather than recommends. Between 1/4 in and 1/2 in it must be BEVELED at a slope no steeper than 1:2, and the practical content of that is arithmetic people skip: a 1:2 slope means the run has to be at least TWICE the rise, so a 1/2 in change needs a full inch of run. A transition strip cut at 1:1 looks beveled and is not, and the test is the run rather than the appearance. Over 1/2 in the change stops being a threshold detail and becomes a RAMP under 405 or 406. That is the expensive sixteenth of an inch: at 1:12 a 5/8 in change needs 7.5 in of run against the 1 in a 1/2 in bevel would have taken, and the run is the small part - a ramp brings landings top and bottom, edge protection, and handrails where the rise exceeds 6 in, none of which a bevel needs. Grinding or shimming the change down to 1/2 in is almost always cheaper than ramping it, which is the decision this tile exists to make visible. Two surface rules ride along. Carpet pile is 1/2 in maximum on a level loop, textured loop, level cut pile, or level cut/uncut pile texture, with exposed edges fastened - and a thick pad under a compliant carpet defeats it just as surely, because the rule is about what a wheel sinks into. Openings must not pass a sphere more than 1/2 in in diameter, and an elongated opening must run PERPENDICULAR to the dominant direction of travel, which is the orientation that decides whether a grate catches a caster or a cane tip. Not checked: whether the surface is stable, firm, and slip resistant under 302.1, which no dimension captures; the ramp itself where one is required - slope, rise per run, landings, edge protection, handrails, and cross slope are 405 and a separate tile; door thresholds, which have their own 1/2 in rule and their own bevel exception at 404.2.5; grating placement relative to a curb ramp or crossing; carpet padding; the accessible route the surface sits on; and state and local accessibility law. A surface screen, not a floor detail.

assumptions.name: Vertical
assumptions.value: 1/4 in high maximum

assumptions.name: Beveled
assumptions.value: over 1/4 in to 1/2 in, at a slope no steeper than 1:2

assumptions.name: Ramped
assumptions.value: greater than 1/2 in, complying with 405 or 406

assumptions.name: Carpet
assumptions.value: pile height 1/2 in maximum

assumptions.name: Openings
assumptions.value: no sphere over 1/2 in; elongated openings perpendicular to the direction of travel

assumptions.name: Ramp slope
assumptions.value: editable; 1:12 is the 405.2 maximum for new construction

solar-times.formula: NOAA's General Solar Position Calculations (the fractional-year Fourier series for declination and the equation of time) give sunrise / sunset / civil / nautical / astronomical twilight from latitude / longitude / date, with the sun's center at zenith 90.833° for sunrise and sunset.
solar-times.edition: NOAA Solar Calculator (Global Monitoring Laboratory), its General Solar Position Calculations, by name. Not the NREL Solar Position Algorithm (Reda & Andreas), which is far more precise.
solar-times.governance: Geometry is not forecasting. Avalanche advisory and incident commander govern.
solar-times.editionNote: Single-edition (NOAA's low-precision series; sunrise and sunset to about a minute at mid-latitudes, less near the poles).

assumptions.name: Atmospheric refraction
assumptions.value: −0.833° standard at horizon

vertical-curve-sight-distance.formula: L = A S^2 / C for S <= L; L = 2 S - C/A for S > L; C = 2158 (SSD crest) or 2800 (passing); K = L/A.
vertical-curve-sight-distance.edition: The AASHTO A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets (the Green Book) crest vertical-curve sight-distance minimums, by name.
vertical-curve-sight-distance.freeAccess: The AASHTO crest-curve length equations are published in the Green Book. AHJ, state DOT design manual, and the licensed civil engineer of record govern.
vertical-curve-sight-distance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
vertical-curve-sight-distance.editionNote: The AASHTO Green Book crest vertical-curve minimums L = A S^2 / 2158 for S <= L and L = 2 S - 2158/A for S > L, the 2158 constant embedding a 3.5 ft driver eye and 2.0 ft object height, the K = L/A rate-of-vertical-curvature form, and that sag curves use headlight/comfort/drainage controls as separate cases. This returns the minimum crest vertical-curve length for the entered stopping sight distance: it is the crest SSD control (passing sight distance uses the larger 2800 constant, and sag curves use headlight/comfort/drainage criteria), takes the SSD as entered, and does not check the drainage-maximum K = 167 or the appearance minimum. A design aid, not a substitute for a licensed civil engineer's design.

assumptions.name: Branch selection
assumptions.value: L = A S^2 / C when S <= L, else L = 2 S - C/A; the governing branch is chosen by the S vs L comparison

assumptions.name: Sight constant
assumptions.value: C = 2158 for the SSD crest (3.5 ft eye, 2.0 ft object); 2800 for passing sight distance

assumptions.name: Crest SSD only
assumptions.value: sag curves use headlight/comfort/drainage criteria, not this relation

motor-feeder-multiple.formula: Feeder conductor (NEC 430.24) >= 1.25 * FLC_largest + sum(FLC_other) + non-motor load. Feeder OCPD (NEC 430.62) <= largest_branch_device + sum(FLC_other), not rounded up (next standard size down where the sum is not a standard rating).
motor-feeder-multiple.edition: Feeder conductor and feeder overcurrent sizing for several motors on one feeder per NEC 430.24 and 430.62, by name; table FLC (not nameplate FLA) per 430.6(A). The AHJ-adopted NEC edition governs.
motor-feeder-multiple.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. Table FLC and branch-device ratings are user-supplied.
motor-feeder-multiple.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
motor-feeder-multiple.editionNote: NEC Articles 430.24 / 430.62 / 430.6(A). The 430.62 feeder device is a maximum and is taken to the next standard size down, never above the code maximum.

assumptions.name: FLC source
assumptions.value: NEC Table 430.250 (etc.) table full-load current, not nameplate FLA

buck-boost-sizing.formula: boost_v = desired_v - supply_v; load_kva = desired_v x load_a / 1000; xfmr_kva = abs(boost_v) x load_a / 1000; ratio% = xfmr_kva / load_kva x 100. The autotransformer is rated for the boost/buck voltage times the load current, a fraction of the full load kVA.
buck-boost-sizing.edition: Single-phase buck-boost (autotransformer) sizing. NEC 2023 Article 450 (transformers); the autotransformer connection per the manufacturer.
buck-boost-sizing.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. Buck-boost selection, the connection diagram, taps, and overcurrent protection are the manufacturer's and the AHJ's; this sizes the required kVA only.
buck-boost-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
buck-boost-sizing.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Autotransformer rating
assumptions.value: rated for the boost/buck voltage (desired minus supply) times the load current, not the full load kVA

assumptions.name: Connection and protection
assumptions.value: the catalog unit, tap connection, and overcurrent protection are manufacturer- and AHJ-governed, not selected here

spray-tip-selection.formula: fan width in = floor(tip / 100) x 2; orifice in = (tip mod 100) / 1000; flow = ref flow x (orifice / ref orifice)^2 x sqrt(psi / ref psi); coverage rate = flow x 1604.1667 / wet mils; travel speed = coverage rate / (fan width / 12).
spray-tip-selection.edition: The airless tip-number convention (fan width at 12 in is the first digit doubled, orifice is the last two digits in thousandths), by name; flow scaled from a calibration tip as the square of the orifice ratio times the square root of the pressure ratio, and coverage from the exact 1,604.17 sq ft per gallon at one mil. Flow and geometry only. The coating manufacturer's recommended tip range, the sprayer manufacturer's data, and airless injection-injury safety requirements govern.
spray-tip-selection.freeAccess: The tip-number convention is public trade practice and the coverage constant is exact arithmetic (231 cubic in per gallon / 0.001 in / 144); the calibration tip's flow is a user-entered manufacturer figure.
spray-tip-selection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
spray-tip-selection.editionNote: An airless tip number is two facts in three digits and both of them matter. Fan width is the first digit doubled, measured at twelve inches from the surface, and it should be matched to the work, because a wide fan on a narrow surface wastes most of the material and a narrow fan on a wall is slow. Orifice is the last two digits in thousandths, and it sets flow, which goes as the square of the orifice -- so a step of a few thousandths is a large change in output, and the orifice also has to be matched to the coating's viscosity, which is why a lacquer tip will not spray block filler. Pressure is the weaker lever because it enters as a square root, so it does far less to flow than changing the tip does and is the wrong knob to reach for. The output that turns all of this into a decision is travel speed, because it is the one number a person has to physically deliver. A tip sized comfortably yields a brisk but normal gun speed; step up two sizes in orifice at the same film build and the required speed exceeds what most people can move a gun smoothly, at which point that tip wants a heavier film or a wider fan and forcing it produces runs. Real flow depends on viscosity and temperature, on pump condition, and on tip wear -- a worn tip passes more material through a wider, softer fan, which is how a job quietly starts running heavy. Transfer efficiency is not modeled and it is not high.

assumptions.name: Orifice squared, pressure square-rooted
assumptions.value: the tip is the strong lever and pressure is the weak one

assumptions.name: Travel speed is the real constraint
assumptions.value: a tip that demands more speed than a person can deliver produces runs

assumptions.name: Tip wear runs a job heavy
assumptions.value: a worn tip passes more material through a wider, softer fan

gas-strut-force.formula: horizontal reach = cg distance x cos(opening angle); lid moment = weight x that reach; force per strut = lid moment / (struts x perpendicular moment arm); the same at a second angle and arm for the comparison.
gas-strut-force.edition: Static moment balance about the hinge -- lid moment against strut moment through its perpendicular moment arm -- by name. Checked at the positions entered; it does not model the gas spring's own force curve, its rise as the rod compresses, or its loss of force in cold weather. The strut manufacturer's force curve, stroke, and mounting recommendations govern.
gas-strut-force.freeAccess: A statics calculation on the user's own geometry; no manufacturer force table is reproduced.
gas-strut-force.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
gas-strut-force.editionNote: Everything is a moment about the hinge. The lid's weight acts at its center of gravity, which for a uniform panel is halfway along it, and the strut pushes along its own line at whatever perpendicular distance the mounting points give it. That perpendicular distance is the moment arm, and it is almost always much shorter than the lid's, which is why struts are rated in the tens or hundreds of pounds for lids that weigh far less. The moment arm is also the design variable and by far the cheapest one to change. Moving the body-side mount farther from the hinge lengthens the arm and reduces the required force substantially; moving it closer shortens the arm and can drive the requirement past anything available, at which point the lid becomes genuinely hard to pull closed. Two struts halve the requirement, which is why almost everything uses a pair. The catch a first-time designer meets is that both moments change through the swing and they do not change at the same rate. The lid's moment falls as it opens, because the horizontal distance to the center of gravity shortens toward zero at vertical, while the strut's arm typically grows and then shrinks. A strut sized only at the closed position may hold the lid there and then fling it open, or hold it open and refuse to close, so the required force belongs checked at more than one position.

assumptions.name: The arm is the design variable
assumptions.value: moving the body-side mount changes the required force far more cheaply than changing the strut

assumptions.name: Both moments vary through the swing
assumptions.value: the lid's falls toward vertical while the strut's arm grows then shrinks; check more than one position

assumptions.name: Force curve not modeled
assumptions.value: a gas spring stiffens as the rod compresses and is noticeably weaker cold

rebar-chair-count.edition: Bar-support count identity by name (chairs on a square grid over the slab area, plus waste); first-principles count arithmetic.
rebar-chair-count.freeAccess: The count arithmetic is public first-principles; the support spacing comes from the spec and CRSI practice.
rebar-chair-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rebar-chair-count.editionNote: Bar supports (chairs and bolsters) hold the rebar or mesh at the specified cover. The support spacing (about 3 to 4 ft each way, tighter under heavy bars to stop sag) comes from the spec and CRSI practice. Distinct from the ties (rebar-tie-wire) and the bars (rebar-weight-takeoff).

assumptions.name: Support spacing
assumptions.value: ~3 to 4 ft each way (default 4 ft); tighter under heavy bars per CRSI

assumptions.name: Grid
assumptions.value: square grid: chairs per unit area = 1 / spacing^2

stairwell-pressurization.formula: airflow_cfm = 2610 x leakage_area_sqft x sqrt(pressure_inwg); door_force_lbf = closer_force + 5.2 x door_width_ft x door_area_sqft x pressure_inwg / (2 x (door_width_ft - knob_setback_ft)); max_pressure_inwg = (force_limit - closer_force) x 2 x (W - d) / (5.2 x W x A).
stairwell-pressurization.edition: Stairwell pressurization airflow from the orifice relation Q = 2610 x A x sqrt(dP) in customary units (cfm, sq ft, in. w.g.), and door opening force from the pressure moment about the hinges taken at the knob's lever arm, by name. The 30 lbf total opening-force cap is the International Building Code / NFPA 92 limit, cited by name and not reproduced. A screen, never a stamp; the smoke-control design, its commissioning test, and a qualified engineer govern.
stairwell-pressurization.freeAccess: Orifice flow and the door moment balance are public physics. The leakage area, design pressure, door geometry, and closer force are the designer's own values; the opening-force limit is entered.
stairwell-pressurization.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
stairwell-pressurization.editionNote: A pressurized stairwell holds a positive pressure difference against the floors so smoke cannot enter, and the air it takes is an orifice problem. Every gap in the enclosure -- door undercuts and edge gaps, construction leakage, penetrations -- passes flow proportional to the square root of the pressure difference, with 2610 the flow coefficient in customary units. That square root is worth noticing, because doubling the design pressure does not double the fan, it multiplies it by about 1.41. The second relation is the constraint that actually decides the design. Pressure across a closed door acts on the whole leaf, and the moment it produces has to be overcome at the knob, which sits on a short lever arm from the hinges. The code caps total opening force and the door closer alone already consumes a third to half of that allowance, so on an ordinary door there is only so much pressure left before a person cannot reliably get out. The usable window between holding smoke back and letting people out is narrow, typically a tenth to a quarter of an inch of water gauge, and the door rather than the fan is what caps it. Raising the design pressure for more smoke margin costs surprisingly little fan and a great deal of door force, which is the trade this puts numbers on.

assumptions.name: Orifice flow
assumptions.value: Q = 2610 x A x sqrt(dP), cfm from sq ft and in. w.g.; flow goes as the SQUARE ROOT of pressure

assumptions.name: Opening-force cap
assumptions.value: 30 lbf total, of which the closer alone typically takes 10 to 15

assumptions.name: The door governs
assumptions.value: the usable design window is roughly 0.10 to 0.25 in. w.g., set by door force rather than by fan capacity

solder-joint-quantity.formula: w_per_in = (PI/4) x wire_dia_in^2 x solder_density_lb_in3; solder_lb = joints x wire_in_per_joint x w_per_in; spools = ceil(solder_lb / spool_lb).
solder-joint-quantity.edition: Solder-weight identity by name (solid-wire cross-section x density x length); first-principles geometry.
solder-joint-quantity.freeAccess: The wire weight is pure geometry (a length of solid wire of known diameter and density); the field wire-per-joint rule is public practice.
solder-joint-quantity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
solder-joint-quantity.editionNote: The wire length per joint is a field rule of thumb (roughly the pipe diameter in inches of 1/8 in solid wire) that varies with cup depth and technique. Lead-free plumbing solder (mostly tin, about 7.3 g/cm^3) runs about 0.265 lb/in^3. The crew buys spools with a spare.

assumptions.name: Wire per joint
assumptions.value: ~the pipe diameter in inches of 1/8 in solid wire; varies with cup depth and technique

assumptions.name: Solder density
assumptions.value: ~0.265 lb/in^3 for lead-free (tin-based) solder; 0.30 is a tin-lead figure

pipe-fitting-takeout.formula: Center-to-center: cut = C-to-C - (takeout_A + takeout_B) + (makeup_A + makeup_B) - (weld_gap_A + weld_gap_B); thread make-up adds back for threaded joints, and a butt-weld root gap is subtracted at each end. Face-to-face lands on the fitting faces, so only make-up (added) and weld gap (subtracted) apply.
pipe-fitting-takeout.edition: Fitting take-out / make-up cut-length layout as taught in NCCER Pipefitting and the standard fitter's references, by name; first-principles.
pipe-fitting-takeout.freeAccess: Public first-principles layout. Fitting take-out and thread make-up are product-/schedule-specific and user-supplied; confirm against your fittings and the spool drawing.
pipe-fitting-takeout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pipe-fitting-takeout.editionNote: Single-edition (first-principles fitter's layout). Center-to-center vs face-to-face is a labeled toggle, never silently mixed. Cross-links rolling-offset and conduit-offset.

assumptions.name: Take-out / make-up
assumptions.value: product- and schedule-specific, user-supplied

fatigue-combined-loading.formula: sigma'a = sqrt((Kf_b sa_b + Kf_ax sa_ax/0.85)^2 + 3 (Kfs ta)^2); sigma'm = sqrt((Kf_b sm_b + Kf_ax sm_ax)^2 + 3 (Kfs tm)^2); sigma'max = sqrt((Kf_b (sa_b + sm_b) + Kf_ax (sa_ax + sm_ax))^2 + 3 (Kfs (ta + tm))^2).
fatigue-combined-loading.edition: Combinations of loading modes for fatigue (Shigley, Mischke and Budynas, Mechanical Engineering Design, Ch. 6), by name: von Mises combination of the notch-corrected alternating and mean components, with the axial alternating stress divided by the axial load factor 0.85 so a rotating-bending endurance limit applies.
fatigue-combined-loading.freeAccess: Standard published fatigue relations; the stress components and notch factors are the user's inputs.
fatigue-combined-loading.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fatigue-combined-loading.editionNote: One alternating and one mean von Mises stress for a part under bending, axial, and torsional load at once, for the Goodman (fatigue-safety-factor) or finite-life check, plus the peak for first-cycle yield. Each mode carries its own notch factor (fatigue-notch-sensitivity). Assumes in-phase loading at one frequency; out-of-phase loading needs a critical-plane method. A design aid; test data govern.

assumptions.name: Combination
assumptions.value: von Mises on the alternating and the mean components separately
assumptions.source: Shigley Ch. 6, combinations of loading modes

assumptions.name: Axial load factor
assumptions.value: axial alternating stress divided by 0.85 (kc) so the bending Se applies

assumptions.name: Phase
assumptions.value: all modes in phase at one frequency

disk-clutch-torque.formula: Uniform wear: T = F mu N (ro + ri)/2. Uniform pressure: T = (2/3) F mu N (ro^3 - ri^3)/(ro^2 - ri^2). Max pressure (uniform wear): p_max = F/(2 pi ri (ro - ri)). N = friction interfaces (single plate = 2).
disk-clutch-torque.edition: The disk-clutch friction torque under the uniform-wear and uniform-pressure assumptions (Shigley, Mechanical Engineering Design, Ch. 16 -- clutches and brakes), by name.
disk-clutch-torque.freeAccess: The clutch-torque equations are standard published machine-design results; the clamp force, friction coefficient, radii, and surface count are the user's inputs.
disk-clutch-torque.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
disk-clutch-torque.editionNote: The friction torque a disk clutch or plate (disk) brake can transmit before slipping, from the axial clamp force F, facing friction mu, outer/inner friction radii ro/ri, and the number of friction interfaces N (a single-plate clutch clamps both faces, N = 2). Uniform WEAR T = F mu N (ro + ri)/2 is the design standard: a facing wears fastest where pressure x velocity is highest, so p x r drives to a constant and the pressure peaks at the inner radius, p_max = F/(2 pi ri (ro - ri)); this gives the lower, conservative torque. Uniform PRESSURE T = (2/3) F mu N (ro^3 - ri^3)/(ro^2 - ri^2) applies to a fresh, rigid facing and runs a little higher. The two converge as the friction ring narrows. The actuating force F is an input (spring or hydraulic cylinder); the heat of engagement is clutch-engagement-energy, the band brake is band-brake-torque, and facing wear life, cone brakes, and self-energizing effects are separate. A design aid; Shigley and the facing maker govern.

assumptions.name: Uniform wear
assumptions.value: T = F mu N (ro + ri)/2, the conservative design value; p max at ri

assumptions.name: Uniform pressure
assumptions.value: T = (2/3) F mu N (ro^3 - ri^3)/(ro^2 - ri^2), fresh rigid facing

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: static torque from F; heat, wear life, band/cone brakes are separate

belt-feeder-capacity.formula: volumetric flow = opening width x opening height x belt speed x 60; tonnage = that volume x bulk density / 2,000; the belt speed for a target tonnage and the gate opening for it invert the same relation.
belt-feeder-capacity.edition: The metering relation for a fixed rectangular gate by name -- a FEEDER's relation, not a conveyor's surcharged-profile one. The feeder manufacturer, a material flow-properties test, and the plant designer govern.
belt-feeder-capacity.freeAccess: Volume and density arithmetic on the user's own geometry and material; no manufacturer table is reproduced.
belt-feeder-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
belt-feeder-capacity.editionNote: A belt feeder is a metering device: the material sits in a hopper and the belt pulls a ribbon out from under it whose cross-section is fixed by the gate opening. Output is therefore linear in speed, which is what makes a feeder controllable, and linear in the opening, which is what makes it adjustable. A conveyor, by contrast, carries whatever is put on it in a surcharged profile, and its capacity relation does not apply here at all. The density check is worth running in the field because it is the quiet way a plant changes its tonnage without changing a setting: the same feeder on a heavier ore delivers proportionally more at exactly the same gate and speed, so a feeder calibrated on one material is not calibrated on another. The failure the arithmetic does not capture is ratholing. A feeder that draws material from only part of the hopper opening creates a flow channel while the rest of the hopper stays static, and the static material eventually consolidates into an arch that stops flow entirely; the fix is an interface that increases in cross-section in the direction of travel, and it is a design feature rather than an adjustment. This does not compute the belt pull or drive power a feeder requires, which is much higher than a conveyor's because the belt is shearing material under a full hopper load.

assumptions.name: A feeder is not a conveyor
assumptions.value: its capacity is a fixed gate cross-section, not a surcharged profile

assumptions.name: Density changes tonnage with nothing touched
assumptions.value: a feeder calibrated on one material is not calibrated on another

assumptions.name: Feeder drive power is much higher than a conveyor's
assumptions.value: the belt shears material under a full hopper load; a common undersizing error

wind-mwfrs-pressure.formula: p_ww = qz G Cp_ww +/- qh GCpi (worst sign); p_lw = qh G Cp_lw +/- qh GCpi (worst sign); p_net = qz G Cp_ww - qh G Cp_lw (internal cancels).
wind-mwfrs-pressure.edition: The ASCE 7-22 Chapter 27 MWFRS design wall pressure p = q G Cp - qi (GCpi), with G = 0.85 (rigid), the wall Cp (+0.8 windward, -0.5 leeward for L/B <= 1), and GCpi = +/-0.18 (enclosed), by name.
wind-mwfrs-pressure.freeAccess: ASCE 7 is available through the ASCE Library at ascelibrary.org; the Chapter 27 Directional-Procedure MWFRS provisions are public.
wind-mwfrs-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wind-mwfrs-pressure.editionNote: The ASCE 7-22 Chapter 27 (27.3.1) MWFRS wall pressure p = q G Cp - qi (GCpi), with G = 0.85 (rigid building), the wall Cp (+0.8 windward, -0.5 leeward for L/B <= 1), and GCpi = +/-0.18 (enclosed). This returns the windward and leeward wall MWFRS pressures (each at the internal-pressure sign that maximizes its magnitude) and the net horizontal design pressure for a rectangular enclosed building; the internal pressure cancels in the net, so the net uses the external difference. It uses the entered qz/qh (from wind-pressure) and wall Cp, G = 0.85 (not the flexible-building Gf), and does not compute the roof MWFRS pressures, the internal-pressure effect on the roof diaphragm, or the torsional (Case 2-4) load patterns. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Wall pressure
assumptions.value: p = q G Cp - qi (GCpi); q = qz windward, qh leeward; G = 0.85 rigid

assumptions.name: Wall coefficients
assumptions.value: Cp = +0.8 windward, -0.5 leeward for a building with L/B <= 1

assumptions.name: Net cancels internal
assumptions.value: the internal pressure acts equally outward on both walls, so the net horizontal pressure is the external difference

injector-size.formula: total_lbh = HP x BSFC; inj_lbh = total_lbh / (n_cyl x duty); inj_ccmin = inj_lbh x 10.5.
injector-size.edition: The fuel-injector-sizing relation lb/h = HP x BSFC / (n_cyl x duty), with the BSFC ranges, the customary 80% duty cycle, and the gasoline cc/min conversion, a standard tuning-reference result, by name.
injector-size.freeAccess: The injector-sizing relation and the BSFC ranges are public results in the engine-tuning references.
injector-size.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
injector-size.editionNote: The injector flow lb/h = HP x BSFC / (n_cyl x duty), the BSFC ranges (~0.45 to 0.50 NA gas, ~0.55 to 0.65 boosted), the customary 80% maximum duty cycle, and the lb/h x 10.5 = cc/min conversion for gasoline (specific gravity ~0.72). This returns the per-injector flow at the stated duty - it uses the entered BSFC (which rises with boost and richer tuning), assumes evenly-distributed port injection with one injector per cylinder, and does not cover a return-versus-returnless fuel system, the rail pressure that sets the injector's static flow, or direct injection. A tuning aid; the engine's measured fueling and the tuner's judgment govern.

assumptions.name: Injector flow
assumptions.value: HP x BSFC divided across the injectors at the maximum duty cycle

assumptions.name: BSFC
assumptions.value: ~0.50 naturally-aspirated gas, 0.55-0.65 boosted; entered by the user

assumptions.name: Conversion
assumptions.value: lb/h x 10.5 = cc/min for gasoline (SG ~0.72)

degree-day-energy.formula: Q = 24 x HDD x UA; fuel = Q/eff; units = fuel / {therm 1e5, oil 138,500, kWh 3,412}; cost = units x price.
degree-day-energy.edition: The degree-day annual-heating-energy method Q = 24 x HDD x UA (base-65 degF) with the fuel and cost conversions, as compiled in the ASHRAE degree-day / RESNET references, by name.
degree-day-energy.freeAccess: The degree-day method and the fuel-energy conversions are public building-science results.
degree-day-energy.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
degree-day-energy.editionNote: The degree-day annual energy Q = 24 x HDD x UA, the base-65 degF heating degree-day convention, the fuel = Q/efficiency, the unit conversions (1 therm = 100,000 Btu, 1 gal fuel oil ~ 138,500 Btu, 1 kWh = 3,412 Btu), and the ASHRAE degree-day / RESNET basis. This returns a degree-day annual-energy and cost estimate - it uses the base-65 degF steady-state degree-day method (a modified/variable-base method with the building's actual balance point is more accurate, and it ignores internal and solar gains that lower the true balance point), takes the UA and local HDD as entered, and does not add cooling, latent, or domestic-hot-water energy. An estimate, not a utility-bill-calibrated model; actual consumption depends on occupancy, weather, and gains.

assumptions.name: Degree-day energy
assumptions.value: Q = 24 x HDD x UA at base-65 degF heating degree-days

assumptions.name: Fuel and cost
assumptions.value: fuel = Q/efficiency, then unit-converted and priced

assumptions.name: Steady-state
assumptions.value: ignores internal and solar gains that lower the true balance point

masonry-limited-access-zone.formula: required limited access zone width = height of the wall to be constructed + 4 ft; the zone runs the entire length of the wall and sits on the side that will be unscaffolded; ground occupied = required width x wall length; bracing is required where the wall height exceeds 8 ft.
masonry-limited-access-zone.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.706, Subpart Q - Concrete and Masonry Construction. A US federal regulation in the public domain, quoted directly.
masonry-limited-access-zone.freeAccess: 29 CFR is published in full at no cost by OSHA and the eCFR.
masonry-limited-access-zone.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
masonry-limited-access-zone.editionNote: The limited access zone is a computed dimension rather than a courtesy margin, and three parts of the sentence get dropped. It scales with the height of the wall TO BE CONSTRUCTED, not with how high the wall stands today - so a 12 ft wall needs a 16 ft zone from the first course, at the moment when there is nothing there yet to fall on anyone. That is precisely why the zone gets set narrow and grown later, and precisely why doing so is wrong: the standard also requires it to be established BEFORE the start of construction of the wall. It runs the ENTIRE length, without qualification, because a wall does not fall only in the middle. And it goes on the side that will be UNSCAFFOLDED, which is the whole point - the scaffolded side has people who are supposed to be there and who are watching the wall; the zone exists for everyone else, and only employees actively engaged in constructing the wall may enter it. The bracing rule has a duration that surprises people. A wall over 8 ft must be adequately braced to prevent overturning and collapse unless it is adequately supported so that it will not, and the bracing shall remain in place until the PERMANENT SUPPORTING ELEMENTS of the structure are in place - not until the mortar cures, not until the crew leaves, but until the building is there to hold the wall up. On most jobs that is long after the masons have finished and moved on, which is when the brace gets removed by someone with no idea what it was holding. Not checked: the design of the bracing itself, which is an engineering question and not a rule of thumb; the adequacy of any alternative support; wall stability during construction and the wind that governs it; protruding reinforcing steel and impalement protection, which is a different section; scaffold design on the working side; mortar and grout strength gain; and whether the wall is a structural element requiring an engineer's involvement. A screen, not a bracing design; Subpart Q and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Zone width
assumptions.value: the height of the wall TO BE CONSTRUCTED plus 4 ft

assumptions.name: Zone length
assumptions.value: the entire length of the wall, without qualification

assumptions.name: Zone side
assumptions.value: the side which will be unscaffolded

assumptions.name: Timing
assumptions.value: established prior to the start of construction of the wall

assumptions.name: Bracing trigger
assumptions.value: walls over 8 ft in height

assumptions.name: Bracing duration
assumptions.value: until the permanent supporting elements of the structure are in place

bandmill-speed-bite.formula: blade speed in surface feet per minute = pi x wheel diameter (in) / 12 x rpm; teeth passing per minute = that speed x 12 / tooth spacing; bite per tooth = feed speed x 12 / teeth per minute; gullet load = bite x kerf x depth of face.
bandmill-speed-bite.edition: Standard sawfiling kinematics by name, with the 0.020 to 0.045 in softwood bite band as sawfiling practice. The saw and mill manufacturers' specifications, a qualified filer, and OSHA govern.
bandmill-speed-bite.freeAccess: Kinematics on the mill's own wheel, tooth, and feed figures; no manufacturer speed-and-feed chart is reproduced.
bandmill-speed-bite.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
bandmill-speed-bite.editionNote: Bite per tooth is what each tooth actually takes and a band's behaviour follows from it. Too small a bite means the tooth is rubbing rather than cutting, which generates heat, work-hardens the tip, and produces the washboard finish that gets blamed on tension; too large a bite overloads the gullet, and a gullet that fills before it exits the cut packs, which is what makes a saw dive. The gullet is the real constraint, and it is why bite and depth of face cannot be considered separately: a bite that is fine in a shallow cant is too much in a deep one, because the gullet has to carry the sawdust across the whole face. That is the arithmetic behind slowing the feed as the cants get bigger, and it is why a mill running mixed sizes at one feed speed has a saw problem on the big logs only. For a filer the useful inversion is the feed speed a target bite implies at the current blade speed and tooth spacing, because feed is a setting the sawyer can act on directly. Gullet capacity is entered rather than derived, since deriving it needs the gullet area and the sawdust bulking factor for the species and moisture. Saw tension, alignment and tracking, tooth geometry, set or swage, blade width and gauge, and strain all matter at least as much as bite and none of them is arithmetic.

assumptions.name: The gullet, not the bite, is the limit
assumptions.value: the same bite in a face two and a half times as deep asks for two and a half times the gullet

assumptions.name: Too little bite is not the safe side
assumptions.value: a rubbing tooth makes heat, dulling, and washboard

assumptions.name: Feed is the setting a sawyer controls
assumptions.value: blade speed and tooth spacing are not adjusted between cants

soft-foot-correction.formula: the rise measured at a foot when that foot alone is loosened, with the other three tight, is the shim that foot needs; the two diagonal sums are compared to separate a single bad foot from a twisted base.
soft-foot-correction.edition: The soft-foot sweep as standard precision maintenance practice, by name. The 0.002 in (0.05 mm) acceptance figure is common practice and is ENTERED rather than fixed. The machine manufacturer's mounting requirements and the plant's precision maintenance procedure govern.
soft-foot-correction.freeAccess: Reading four indicator numbers the millwright takes; no manufacturer table is reproduced.
soft-foot-correction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
soft-foot-correction.editionNote: Every alignment number is a lie until soft foot is zero, because a machine that rocks changes shape when the bolts come down. If a loosened foot springs up, the bolt was pulling the machine onto a gap and distorting the frame, and the shim to add is exactly the rise. Working ONE foot at a time isolates each, and repeating the sweep matters because correcting one redistributes the others. Two kinds hide behind the same reading: parallel soft foot is a plain gap and takes a flat shim, angular soft foot is a foot not parallel to the base and takes a stepped or machined shim -- a flat shim under an angular foot only moves the contact point. The diagonal check separates a bad foot from a bad base: 1, 7, 2 and 1 mils give diagonals of 2 and 9, and the whole 7 mil disagreement sits on the one foot. A twisted base instead spreads the rise across a diagonal pair. Aligning before the shim goes in produces a beautiful set of cold readings that change the moment the bolts are torqued.

assumptions.name: Parallel versus angular is an indication, not a determination
assumptions.value: that needs a feeler gauge or a step check

assumptions.name: Grout, base and anchor bolts are not evaluated
assumptions.value: voided grout is a common root cause shimming will not fix

assumptions.name: Pipe strain produces the same symptom
assumptions.value: and is not cured by shims

dry-hop-beer-loss.formula: hops = rate x barrels (31 gal); absorbed = hops x gal per lb; packages lost = absorbed / package size.
dry-hop-beer-loss.edition: Pellets retain roughly 0.5 to 1.5 gal per lb. The brewery's own measured absorption governs.
dry-hop-beer-loss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dry-hop-beer-loss.editionNote: Absorption is linear, so doubling the rate doubles the loss exactly. Hop creep is controlled by time and temperature with gravity confirmed stable before packaging.

assumptions.name: Recovery
assumptions.value: no beer recovered from the hop bed

galvanize-kettle-throughput.formula: cycle = lower + immerse + withdraw and drain + travel; lifts per hour = 60 / cycle in minutes; crane throughput = lifts per hour x load per lift; heat demand = lb/h x specific heat x (bath temperature - ambient); heat-limited throughput = burner output to the steel / (specific heat x temperature rise); the LOWER of the two governs.
galvanize-kettle-throughput.edition: The kettle cycle throughput relation and the sensible heat demand of the steel, with ASTM A123 named for the coating the immersion time is chosen to produce. Immersion time and burner output are ENTERED.
galvanize-kettle-throughput.freeAccess: A cycle-time relation and a sensible-heat relation.
galvanize-kettle-throughput.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
galvanize-kettle-throughput.editionNote: A KETTLE IS TWO MACHINES IN SERIES WITH DIFFERENT LIMITS -- a crane whose rate is the cycle and a thermal machine whose rate is the burners -- and quoting one tons-per-hour figure for the plant hides which is binding, so both are computed and the lower is reported. Heavy work gives MORE tons per hour despite a far longer immersion, because the load per lift grows faster than the cycle does, while the same comparison in square feet per minute goes the OTHER way. Both are real: zinc, dross and coating quality follow AREA and the invoice follows WEIGHT. On heavy work the burners usually govern, and the shortfall against the crane-cycle promise is reported rather than left implicit. THE REMEDY IS BURNER CAPACITY OR SCHEDULING, NOT A HOTTER BATH: raising bath temperature accelerates kettle wall attack, and a kettle failure is the most expensive event a galvanizing plant has. This heat figure covers only heating the steel -- wall losses, ash and dross, reheating the zinc the work removes and flux evaporation are all beyond it, so the burner capacity actually needed exceeds it.

assumptions.name: Immersion time is entered
assumptions.value: a metallurgical requirement set by section, chemistry, bath temperature and specification
assumptions.source: the galvanizer's own cycle and coating records

assumptions.name: Steel specific heat
assumptions.value: about 0.12 Btu/lb-degF, entered and adjustable

assumptions.name: Only the steel is heated
assumptions.value: wall losses, dross, flux and zinc reheat are not counted
assumptions.source: the kettle and burner manufacturers' data
